In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the production of direct photons in heavy-ion collisions, with emphasis on the effects due to the hot and dense matter created in these events.
the development of the reaction operator formalism and its applications to direct photon production in relativistic heavy ion collisions.

the development of a theoretical framework for a systematic study of photon emission in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, which is essential to the understanding of the quark–glon plasma phase transition and to the extraction of the transport properties of quarks and gluons in the hot and dense matter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed direct photon yield is not modified by the hot and dense medium.
direct photons provide no evidence for a hot quark–glulon plasma in heavy ion collisions at s = 62 GeV and 0%–20%, while at s = 200 GeV and 20%–60% a hot quark matter phase might be created.
the direct photon cross sections in heavy ion collisions are not modified by final-state interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
direct photon production in high energy heavy ion collisions is not a clean probe of the hot and dense medium created in these reactions.
direct photon production is a clean probe for the initial-state nuclear effects, but it is not a good observable to investigate the hot and dense medium formed in heavy ion collisions at RHIC.
the photon bremsstrahlung is an interesting effect, but that its contribution to direct photons at the RHIC is not large.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bremsstruhlung contribution to the direct photon spectrum is small and that the direct photon spectrum at high transverse momentum can be used to probe the nuclear gluon distribution at high x.

the bremsstruhlung photon yield is suppressed by a factor of 2–3 in the region 2 GeV < p T < 5 GeV, compared to the yield in p + p collisions, and that this suppression is not compensated by the enhancement of the initial-state nuclear effects.
